title: The first screen of a scheduling product
metaTitle: Scheduling product UX: the first screen
excerpt: Open a scheduling screen on the next free time and one action that takes it. Guests should see that time before any account, tour, or feature list.
alt: A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung industrial lamps, and a mirror, a first view that puts the thing you came for in the open.
caption: The goods are on the floor before any explanation. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a scheduling product show?
faqs.answer: Show the next time someone can take, with the person or service, the length, the time zone, and the place. The action should use one verb that matches what the system will do, either holding the slot or requesting it. An account, a tour, and a plan comparison can wait until a time is on screen.

faqs.question: Should a guest create an account before seeing open times?
faqs.answer: No. Show the open times first. Ask for an email when you need somewhere to send the invite, and ask for a password only if you truly need an account after a time is chosen. A returning person can see their next booking above those times without the page becoming a dashboard.

faqs.question: How should a full week behave?
faqs.answer: Say that nothing is open, and say when the next opening is, with a way to jump there. Offer a waitlist or a note to the host if that is a real path. An empty grid with no sentence looks broken, and clicking through blank weeks is a navigation problem the first screen can prevent.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The job of scheduling product ux is to open on the next time a person can take, and on one action that takes it. The visitor wants a time, not an account, and the first screen is there to show that object.

Nielsen Norman Group's study of how long people stay on web pages found that visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns a longer look. Spend that window on a tour and the time they came for never appears.

## The object is a time

Name the thing on the screen before you name the product. For a person booking a conversation, the object is an open slot: who it is with, how long it lasts, and a clock time that is still free. For a room, a court, or a service, the object is the same shape with a different noun. The product name can sit in the corner. It should not be the headline.

Write the headline as a fact the visitor can check. "Alex has three openings this week" is a fact. "Scheduling, simplified" is a slogan, and a slogan does not tell them whether Thursday exists. If several people can be booked, the first choice is the person or the service, and the times appear the moment that choice is made. Do not hide the calendar behind a paragraph about the company.

Show the zone in words beside the times. If the visitor's zone differs from the host's, show both. Duration belongs on the slot itself: 25 minutes, 50 minutes, a site visit. When two lengths exist, they are a choice on this screen. A length that appears only after an account is created is a surprise, and surprises are how a sure booking turns into a closed tab.

Host rules such as buffers, minimum notice, and how far ahead a guest may book should already be applied. The guest needs the result: which times are actually open. A tooltip about the rule is optional. A calendar full of times that fail on the next step is a broken first screen.

## One action, and what it is allowed to promise

Pick one verb and keep it. Take this time, or request this time. If the click holds the slot, say that it is held, and say for how long. If the click only notifies the host, say that the host still has to confirm. A button that says Book, followed by a screen that says Request pending, teaches the visitor that the product cannot be trusted with the next step either.

The form after the click should ask only what the host needs in order to hold the meeting or prepare for it. A name, a way to reach them, and the reason, when the reason changes the meeting. Payment belongs in that same short path when payment is part of taking the time. It should not arrive as a second product on a later page.

Leave the rest off this screen. A feature tour, a blog, a plan comparison, a login wall, a modal that offers to "show you around," the host's notification settings, the list of integrations. The host's story can live on the company site. This screen is the booking. Got Next and Leadly are public examples of product interfaces that stay on one job. A scheduling screen should be that strict. If a block does not help someone see or take a time, it waits.

## Guests first, accounts later

Most first visits are guests. Show open times before you ask anyone to create an account. Many hosts need an email and nothing else. A password, a company name, and a marketing opt-in, asked before a single slot is visible, answer a question the visitor has not asked. They came to see if a time exists.

A returning person with a session can be greeted by name, with their next booking above the open times and a clear way to move or cancel it. Keep that strip small. The open times are still the page. Merging "your upcoming meeting" and "book a new one" into one crowded hero makes both jobs harder to see.

If you do need an account, ask for it after a time has been chosen, and say why. "We will send the calendar invite here" is a reason. "Create your free account to continue" is a wall. Hold the slot while they finish, and tell them the hold will expire. A slot that disappears in silence feels like a bug.

## Empty, loading, and the week that is full

If nothing is open, say so in a sentence and offer the next useful step. Join a waitlist, ask for a later week, or write the host. An empty grid with no sentence looks broken. A spinner that never resolves looks broken. Name the state in the same voice as the rest of the page: short, specific, and free of apology theater.

Loading should show the shape of the week, not a blank white card. People decide quickly whether the page knows what they came for. A skeleton of days, with the host's name already visible, tells them they are in the right place while the times arrive. A full-screen animation of a calendar icon tells them nothing.

When the week is full, say when the next opening is, even if it is three weeks out. Offer to jump there. Forcing someone to click through empty weeks is a navigation failure you will then have to solve with search. The first screen can do this job itself.

## Time, place, and the meeting they think they are booking

Say where the meeting happens before the click. A video link, a phone call, an address, or "the host will confirm the place." People book the wrong thing when the place is a footnote under a success message. If a video link is generated only after confirmation, say that too.

If the host offers more than one kind of meeting, the kinds are the first choice, in the host's language. "Intro call," "working session," "on-site measure." Each kind can carry its own length, place, and questions. Do not make the guest discover the difference after they have already picked a clock time.

Questions on the form should be few, and each one should change something: how the host prepares, which person it is routed to, or whether the slot is even appropriate. A form of twelve fields on a 25-minute intro is a different product from the one the first screen promised. Cut until every field has a reason you could say out loud.

## The host's first screen is a different object

The person taking a time and the person offering times do not share a first screen. The guest's object is the next opening. The host's object is the next meeting that needs them, plus anything that will break the page if they ignore it: a calendar that stopped syncing, a hold about to expire, a question they still have to answer. Put that on the host's home. Do not give the host the public booking page and call it a dashboard.

Keep host tools one step away, labeled as tools. Editing weekly hours, connecting a calendar, and changing the questions on the form are settings. They are a cabinet. They are not the first thing a host should parse on a Tuesday morning. If the only way to see today's meetings is to open the public page in a private window, the product has mixed up its two users.

When a team shares a booking page, say whose time is being offered. A round-robin that hides the person until after the click is fine when the visitor asked for "anyone on the team." It is a trust problem when the visitor asked for a named person and received someone else. The first screen should match the promise in the link they were sent.

Trade Moai is a public example of an interface organized so a person can scan. Steal that discipline for the host view: a short list, the next meeting at the top, and a status line if something needs a human. A wall of charts about "booking conversion" can wait until the host has asked for it. The morning job is to know what is happening today.

## What to review before you ship the screen

Read the first screen on a phone, with real times, in a zone that is not yours. Check four things. The next open time is visible without scrolling past a tour. The verb matches what the system will do. The zone and the place are stated. A guest can reach a confirmation without inventing a password they will forget.

Then try the empty week, the full week, and a slot that gets taken between click and confirm. That last case is an error, and it deserves its own words. [Errors in a scheduling product](/blog/errors-in-a-scheduling-product) is the next piece to write, because a clear first screen still loses the booking if the failure is a code and a sad illustration.

On a Hanabi project this screen is drawn in Figma against a real week of times, then built in the browser, where the zone label, the button, and the type can be judged at the width a guest will actually use. We design and build, in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with Tailwind for layout. Motion is for the moment a hold is confirmed, not for introducing the product. Availability, holds, and the booking record belong in data, which is why Prisma and PostgreSQL fit this job, with the public page served so the times feel immediate.

If your booking screen still opens on a tour, or the times sit behind an account, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the object you believe the visitor wants. The call should settle whether that object is a time, a person, or a request, and what the one action is allowed to promise.
